newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries off sharply, rate hike fears mount.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries off sharply, rate hike fears mount.

text.p: Renewed fears of a near-term tightening by the Federal Reserve on Friday sent U.S. Treasury prices tumbling and yields soaring to levels not seen in more than three months.

Just before midday, the 30-year bond was at 95-6/32, down 1-19/32 from late Thursday. Its yield jumped to 6.88 percent from 6.75 percent. The bond was as high as 6.90 percent, its highest point since closing at 6.92 percent on September 30.
The two-year note was down 8/32 at 99-13/32 to yield 6.07 percent, its highest since closing at 6.92 on September 30.

The huge selloff was triggered by a much stronger than expected December employment report. The Labor Department said nonfarm payrolls rose 262,000 in December after growing by a revised 127,000 in November. A Reuters poll earlier in the week had forecast a 192,000 rise.
Meanwhile, average hourly earnings rose six cents, or 0.5 percent -- more than double the jump expected -- and the factory workweek rose 0.3 hours to 34.8.
Treasuries immediately dove more than a point, later extending losses to nearly two points, before light buying brought the market off its intraday lows.
"It pretty much sealed the fate the Fed may have to tighten at its next meeting February 4 and 5," said Michael McClure, head trader at Zions First National Bank.
Analysts said the latest economic news, which follows strong data last week, ensures Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in the fourth quarter well above 3.0 percent.

"I don't think people (in the market) are comfortable with that," said Craig Coats, co-head of taxable fixed income trading at Prudential Securities Inc. "People are now having meetings as to what they are going to do."

The near-term outlook, though, does not appear that rosy, players said. "We are faced with a lot of supply, so if we don't get a trading bounce (before closing) today, the market will be in severe trouble next week," Coats said.
Market participants noted that the days of two-year notes below 6.0 percent and bonds at 6.75 percent are largely over.

"We had a repricing rather than a panic," said James Winder, money market economist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc. "I don't know that we will see Fed tightening soon. But (the strong jobs report) puts the Fed more in play than it has been since September."

As fears of a rate hike mount, traders said new ranges have been established. The 30-year bond is seen trading between 6.80 and 6.95 percent, although some see the bond climbing as high as 7.10 percent in the next few weeks. The two-year note is seen ranging 6.0 to 6.25 percent.
"I wouldn't be surprised if the two-year note is auctioned at 6.15 percent" at its next sale, Coats said, adding that the subsequent five-year note could come in at 6.50 percent.
Traders were worried Japanese accounts may begin to sell Treasuries, since a weak yen coupled with faltering Tokyo stocks may make it difficult for banks to write off bad loans.
Amid the selling, traders reported some buying during the morning -- primarily in short and intermediate paper -- but the selling pressure was too much.

According to GovPx, trading volume in the morning was very robust, with $25 billion traded in the first hour after the employment report was released. A record $87.8 billion was traded by 1230 EST/1530 GMT, well above the average of $48 billion by midday on a typical Friday in the first quarter and above an average of $56 billion by midday on an employment Friday in 1996.
Trading was heaviest in the two-year note, with a record $11.7 billion traded by midday, followed by $7.8 billion in five-year notes. Volume in 30-year bonds was $1.2 billion.
